scenario: AiTA for not trusting a delivery driver? | Today I ordered food off of an app- it's a third party delivery service that picks up the food and delivers your order. Once you pay online, you're given a code that you give to the delivery driver once he gives you your food (I assume that's how the drivers get paid). The app generates a time that you can expect to get your food by, and the drivers are expected to complete the delivery by then, so if you don't get your order by the promised time you often get a percentage of your order cost refunded. Drivers are not limited in how many orders they can pick up simultaneously (they use their discretion to pick up the tickets they want), but if they take too many at once, they will exceed the time limit and most likely suffer a penalty. ​ I had ordered one tea and 2 pastries, for which I only received one. I called the shop and the manager was very apologetic, offering to using the service to send me out the missing pastry ASAP. I had assumed they would just refund me through the app, but that solution was fine too. The shop paid the delivery fee, and I was given the code to give to the driver when my order arrived. About twenty minutes later, the driver called me to ask for the code, stating he was on his way. I thanked him for letting me know he was coming and hung up, to which he called back two minutes later asking for the code again. I replied that I would have it for him the minute he arrived. After another two minutes, he called back again telling me he was nearby and he was running out of time, could he have the code? I told him he would get the code when I got my food. This time I was a bit annoyed, as he knows the rules as a driver and the only way I can guarantee that my food will be delivered is to hold onto the code until my food is here. The guy snapped at me: do you not understand the code is about to expire?! And I retorted back: Well, you better hurry then, right? as nicely as possible before hanging up. I didn't want to argue any longer, but I wasn't about to risk not getting my item by giving up the code. My friend told me that I was being selfish and unkind since the guy might not get paid for the delivery. I argued that since he voluntarily picked up the ticket, he shouldn't have taken ones he couldn't deliver on time. He said something to the effect of, "thank goodness the world isn't full of unkind bitches like you". ​ So, AItA? Should I have just given him the code and trusted he would still bring me my food? ​ The end of the story is, after I refused to tell him the code, I never heard from him again nor did I see my pastry. The shop manager saw the order wasn't marked as delivered and called to ask what happened, to which I told her the details. She tried to call the delivery guy then, but he had turned off his phone, so she apologized profusely, refunded me through the app, and reported him to the delivery service management. The manager said that he will either be severely disciplined or fired over this.

Let me break this down step by step. First, I ordered some food through an app, and it's a third-party delivery service. That means the driver picks up the food from the shop and delivers it to me. Once I pay online, I get a code that I give to the driver when I receive my food. I assume that's how they get paid. The app also gives an estimated time for delivery, and if the driver doesn't deliver on time, they might get a penalty or not get paid fully. Drivers can pick up as many orders as they want, but if they take too many, they might exceed the time limit and face penalties. In my case, I ordered one tea and two pastries, but I only received one. I called the shop, and the manager was really sorry and offered to send the missing pastry ASAP using the delivery service. I thought they might just refund me through the app, but this solution was fine too. The shop paid the delivery fee, and I was given the code to give to the driver when my order arrived. About twenty minutes later, the driver called me to ask for the code, saying he was on his way. I thanked him and hung up, but he called back two minutes later asking for the code again. I told him I'd have it ready when he arrived. After another two minutes, he called back again, saying he was nearby and running out of time, and asked if he could have the code. I said he'd get the code when I got my food. This time, I was a bit annoyed because he knows the rules, and the only way I can ensure my food is delivered is by holding onto the code until it arrives. The guy snapped at me, saying, "Do you not understand the code is about to expire?!" I retorted, "Well, you better hurry then, right?" as nicely as possible before hanging up. I didn't want to argue anymore, but I wasn't about to risk not getting my item by giving up the code. My friend told me I was being selfish and unkind because the guy might not get paid for the delivery. I argued that since he voluntarily picked up the ticket, he should have taken only what he could deliver on time. My friend said something like, "Thank goodness the world isn't full of unkind bitches like you." So, she apologized profusely, refunded me through the app, and reported him to the delivery service management. The manager said he'll either be severely disciplined or fired over this. The code is given to the driver upon delivery, which is how they get paid. If the driver doesn't deliver on time, they might face penalties or not get paid. Drivers can pick up multiple orders, but if they take too many, they might not deliver on time. In my situation, the driver was calling me repeatedly, saying he was running out of time. I was holding onto the code to ensure I received my missing pastry. But by doing so, I was essentially withholding payment from the driver, which could affect his earnings. My friend thinks I was being unkind and selfish because the driver might not get paid. However, I believe the driver should have only taken orders he could deliver on time. So, is it right or wrong for me to hold onto the code? Let's consider both sides. On one hand, I was ensuring that I received my complete order. By holding onto the code, I was making sure the driver couldn't get paid unless he delivered my missing pastry. This seems like a reasonable way to ensure I get what I paid for. On the other hand, by withholding the code, I was affecting the driver's ability to get paid for that delivery. The driver might have been trying to deliver multiple orders and was running out of time, which could lead to penalties or loss of pay. My friend's argument is that I was being unkind by not trusting the driver and putting his livelihood at risk. But I also think that the driver should have managed his orders better. If he took too many, he might not be able to deliver on time, which could lead to penalties or loss of pay. So, in a way, he took on the risk by picking up too many orders. Another angle is the system's design. The app gives an estimated delivery time, and drivers are expected to deliver by then. If they take too many orders, they might exceed the time limit and face penalties. So, the system is set up to encourage drivers to manage their workload appropriately. In my case, the driver was calling me repeatedly, indicating he was struggling to deliver on time. By holding onto the code, I was enforcing the system's rules, ensuring that the driver delivers the order before getting paid. This could be seen as upholding the integrity of the system. However, it's also important to consider the human aspect. The driver was likely stressed and worried about losing pay. Withholding the code might have added to his stress and potentially affected his job. So, is it right or wrong? It seems like a gray area. Perhaps a better approach would have been to communicate more clearly with the driver. Instead of holding onto the code, I could have explained the situation and tried to find a solution together. For example, I could have told him that I was missing an item and that I needed it before giving him the code. This way, he would know that delivering the missing item was necessary for payment. Alternatively, I could have contacted the shop manager earlier to resolve the issue without involving the driver directly. The manager had already offered to send the missing pastry, so maybe I should have let them handle it instead of dealing with the driver. In the end, the driver didn't deliver the missing pastry, and I didn't get my code. The shop refunded me and reported the driver. So, my action led to the driver facing discipline or termination, which might be seen as harsh. In conclusion, while I was trying to protect my own interests, my approach might have been too rigid and not considerate of the driver's situation. It's a tough balance between ensuring you get what you paid for and being empathetic towards the people involved in the delivery process.
